newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac extends influence at Bank of France.
newsitem.headline: Chirac extends influence at Bank of France.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac on Friday named two allies to the Bank of France's monetary policy council in a move which could tip the balance of power in the central bank towards faster interest rate cuts.

The government said it had named Pierre Guillen, 69, and Jean-Rene Bernard, 64, to the council, replacing two men who had been regarded as staunch supporters of hawkish Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet.

The government played down talk of a change in policy at the central bank, and economists ruled out any threat to France's decade-old policy of linking the franc to the mark -- seen as the cornerstone of the future European single currency.

Chirac and the government made a point of reaffirming on Friday their confidence in the Bank's ability to conduct monetary policy "in stability and continuity", government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said.
"There will be no revolution at the monetary policy council," council member Paul Marchelli told Reuters.
But economists said the appointments could nonetheless shift the bias in favour of slightly faster interest rate cuts to boost the economy and tackle record 12.7 percent unemployment.

"The nominations which have just been made at the Bank of France clearly signify one thing, that a decision has been made to bring French short-term rates below German rates in the coming months," Jean-Michel Naulot, a banker close to parliament president and veteran anti-Maastricht campaigner Philippe Seguin, told Reuters.

It also increases Chirac's leverage over the independent Bank of France, until now dominated by Trichet, nicknamed "the Ayatollah" of the strong franc for his tough insistence on protecting the stability of the franc even at the cost of raising interest rates if necessary.

Chirac sparred with Trichet over policy during the 1995 presidential election campaign. And his decision to put new men into the Bank was seen as a blow to the governor, who political sources say had sought the reappointment of one of the outgoing members, ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat.
"It's a signal to Trichet, putting in people who won't follow him blindly, even if there's no change in monetary policy," said Jean-Louis Mourier of Louis Dreyfus Finance.

Economists said they did not expect any radical change in the Bank's policy of steadily lowering interest rates, while also keeping a close eye on the level of German rates to ensure the franc-mark exchange rate remained stable.

And Lamassoure, who is also budget minister, stressed that official interest rates in France were no longer an obstacle to economic growth, whereas some 15 months ago -- when they were at much higher levels --they had been the "principal handicap".
"It is not the level of interest rates that is slowing economic growth," he told reporters.

But economists said the new appointments now made them question whether the Bank of France might try to take French rates below German rates -- seen as unlikely before in the face of strong resistance from Trichet.
At 3.15 percent the Bank of France's key intervention rate is slightly above the benchmark German repo rate of 3.0 percent.

The link between German and French rates -- as with the link between the franc and the mark -- is seen as a key to the convergence of Europe's two biggest economies in the run up to their union in a single currency from January 1, 1999.

"The Bank of France is likely to cut rates faster than before," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said. "Whether the Bank of France could try to cut rates below the German level is now an open question, whereas before it was not."
"What we can do, and perhaps the new nominations will allow this, is to accelerate the reduction of official rates," Marchelli said.
The appointment of Guillen, ex-deputy head of the CNPF employers' federation, is likely to reinforce a minority wing in the Bank, including Marchelli, who have argued for lower rates.
Guillen is close to Marchelli and seen as more dovish on monetary policy than the outgoing members.
Political sources said there was previously a six-to-three majority backing Trichet, including the governor himself.
The new line-up could create a four-to-four balance, with Bernard, whose son-in-law is deputy secretary general in Chirac's office, the swing member of the council.
Marchelli, however, played down any talk of a shift in the balance of power in the Bank of France, arguing that each member made his or her own choice in rates depending on circumstances.
"You should not believe that the monetary policy council is divided in two camps," he said.
"The men and woman on the council try to work in the most objective way possible, without taking account of external pressure. The council is not a place for politicking," he said.

He noted that according to the law which made the Bank independent in 1994, Trichet held the casting vote in the event of a tie. But even Trichet was capable of modifying his position when this appeared appropriate, he said. "He took part in the (recent) reduction in interest rates."
